caption: “The lowest moments usually come from people who love you but don’t understand you. They see you struggling, and say: ‘Why don’t you just stop doing it?’ But if they knew how important it was to me, they would never ask that. I had a little success in my late twenties. I was part of a band that signed to a record label, but we never had any hit music. It was mainly local stuff. Most of my thirties was working two jobs, struggling to pay bills, playing a late-night slot on a Tuesday night in a room with no people there, or maybe just a couple of my friends. It’s not that I felt disrespected, just not noticed. I guess obscure would be a good word. You’re lugging your guitar around everywhere. Nothing’s happening. It feels like you’re trying to hammer a nail with a banana. Those are the years where you say: ‘Man, is this really what I want to be doing? Can I live like this and be happy?’ But every time I tried to put my guitar down, I’d find myself writing a poem, or writing a lyric, or trying to write a riff. Turns out that I did need to be creative to be happy, more than I needed to be successful. It’s been a long journey. It’s like any other small business; you’ve got to build it one brick at a time. Even though my thirties were some tough years, it was during those years that my songwriting began to improve incredibly. Really talented musicians began to notice, and they were like: ‘Man, I love your stuff. I want to be in your band.’ That’s when it all started to come together. My current band is called @tentonmojo. We’re playing a show tonight, and there will probably be like 80 or 100 people there. I’m forty-three, and I’m finally putting out stuff that other people are relating to. You know how music has this way of sinking into your memory, and becoming connected to a certain time in your life? I’m hoping that might happen tonight for some of those eighty people. With my music, finally.”

caption: “Two days ago I walk into the water, and two ladies from Ukraine, from my native city, they say: ‘Captain. Oh, Captain.’ Then they ask me how old I am. I tell them, guess; and one of them gives me 55-60. The other gives me 60-65. So I say to them, and I’m saying this to you: On January 1st, God willing, I will turn 87. Today I have problem with my knee, but two years ago I could swim to Coney Island and back. I tell you my secret. Every day—one shot of vodka. One shot, no more. Every winter—skiing. Every summer—playing soccer, here on the beach. And you must work. Work keeps you on the surface of life. Without work you will sink down into your mind: ‘I don’t like this, I don’t want this, I can’t do this.’ You will drown there. So you must work. Nothing to make you rich, but enough to stay on the surface.”

caption:
Dear New York, 

We’re honored to be part of @HumansofNY's exhibition that turns Grand Central Station into a living tribute to the city’s people and stories.

From October 6–19, Juilliard students and alumni will perform 50-minute piano concerts under the celestial ceiling of @grandcentralnyc’s main concourse. Juilliard’s collaboration with Humans of New York is bringing hundreds of thousands of commuters and visitors into contact with unexpected, inspiring musical moments each day.

Performer lineup and schedule in bio. 

Love, 
Juilliard

caption: “Our first daughter’s name is Ashley. It’s a weird name in a Russian community. But she was the first American baby in our family, and we wanted an American name. We decided that if we ever had another daughter, her name would be Abigail. I’ve always loved that name. But we weren’t in a rush to get pregnant again. I was young. And we never predicted that we’d have all these struggles. It wasn’t until the miscarriage that we decided to try fertility treatments. By then Ashley was already twelve. It was one of the most difficult periods of my life: the cycles, the shots. You keep going through the motions, hoping something good will happen. It steals all the joy from your current life. Eventually the doctors told us there was a zero percent chance without IVF, so we decided to give up and focus on our little family of three. Ashley promised me if she ever had a daughter, she’d name her Abigail. There was a bit of a grieving process; I’d spent so long envisioning the baby. But we focused on making Ashley’s childhood as special as possible. I tried to create little traditions. We always watched Fiddler on the Roof the night before Yom Kippur. And on the first day of school, I’d always cook chicken soup. Even after Ashley went to college, I would send her off to school with chicken soup. During her senior year I began to not feel well. At first I thought COVID, because it was during the pandemic. Then I thought early menopause, because I was forty-one already. But one sleepless night I found a box of pregnancy tests that had expired ten years earlier. They still worked. I used all ten of them, and each time there was the bright pink line. There was no joy at first. I was so afraid of having another miscarriage. It was a very difficult pregnancy, so I made a deal with God. I don’t know why, but I promised him that if I could carry to term, I wouldn’t color my hair until the birth. By the time she came my hair was very, very gray. How do I even describe it? So much joy. It’s a second season, a second wind. A few years ago we were preparing for early retirement. But now we’re busier than ever: planning a wedding for Ashley, and looking at preschools for Abigail."
firstComment: SAME! Went through IVF, it was Hell, for years. Finally my doctor encouraged me to stop. I had a nearly zero percent chance. No other children. Devastated. I picked my 40th as the day I would put the hope away.  6 months later I was staring at a positive pregnancy test. My reaction was laughter and "are you fucking SERIOUS right now?" 😂 Life will work out, always. My daughter is now 6 and the love of my life. But I also look back on that struggling woman taking all those shots and I wish I could tell her "you are enough on your own." Its hard to explain, when you struggle with infertility for so long and then are blessed. It is the most beautiful thing, but you are also finally able to look back at your old self and realize, "that was beautiful, too."

caption: “The first time it happened was at a music festival. I was fourteen. I’m not sure why my parents let me go; I don’t think they understood what a music festival crowd really entailed. These two women came up to me and were like: ‘We think you have a great look. Have you ever thought about modeling?’ And after that I started getting scouted a lot. I was a creative kid; I also got praised for my artwork. But I got more praise, more consistently, for my physical appearance. It gave me these grand ideas of the future. All throughout high school, I was like: ‘I’m moving to New York. I’m going to be a model. And then all these people who think I’m weird—they’ll see that I was onto something this whole time.’ Those first couple years after graduation I went to a lot of castings. I got a few jobs here and there. Nothing too big. I noticed that a lot of the most successful models had some sort of safety net. They didn’t have to work nine-to-five jobs. They could spend money on good, clean foods. They could go to the gym all the time. I had to work a more reliable job to survive, and then all this other stuff started happening. My first real romantic relationship fell apart. The cat I loved like a son passed away. All this stuff that had felt so solid started falling apart. And this lifelong dream thing, the thing I’d been banking on to get me out of being a freak—it wasn’t working out. For awhile I turned very nihilistic; it was like: why me? But also, at the same time: why not me? Why did I think I was so special? I felt so stupid and naive for believing everything I was ever told. For believing I could be anything different than what I always thought I was. But a friend told me something, that really stuck with me. He said that everybody has to give up on certain dreams in life. And it’s true. The more people you meet, the more you see in the way of broken dreams. It seems like almost everyone is coming to terms with something they expected to happen, but didn’t. And there’s a comfort in that. At least that’s what I’ve been telling myself. It’s a whole lot better than being like: ‘This didn’t work out. I’m doomed forever.’”

caption: “It’s a weird time. I’ve still got to get to work on time, pay my bills, manage chronic illness, all that stuff, while the world in general seems to be falling apart. It can be a challenge to juggle those two things while making sure one of them doesn’t completely destroy my mental health. It’s just an odd thing to be like: ‘Oh, all of these atrocities are being committed in Gaza with my tax dollars, but what am I going to eat for dinner?’ Or: ‘Trump just dismantled another check on his power. We’re slowly sliding into fascism, he’s winning at every turn, nobody’s stopping him— but what concert should we go to this weekend?’ The strangest part about the whole thing is that we’ve never been so connected. I could understand if this was eighty years ago; news travelled slowly. But now, in an instant, you get these facts, photos, videos. Verified by credible news, verified by aid organizations, verified by the United Nations—and nobody cares. Well, a lot of people care. But the people who can actually fix things: who can make a call, set up a meeting, post to millions of followers—they don’t care. Instead of standing up for the voiceless, they’d rather lay low, keep their head down, cling to their money or status. So yeah, it’s hard to be a person who cares right now. Sometimes you just want to melt into your bed or couch and be with your feelings. But I won’t say that I feel hopeless. I’d never say that, because that’s what they want—those people who only care about winning, who don’t care about collateral damage. They want people to feel powerless. And I’m not going to give them that luxury. There are still reasons to be hopeful. Zohran just won the primary. And that’s a sign of change, in New York City at least. Even the people who don’t agree with his politics have to admit: his campaign was built on community. It wasn’t funded by billionaires. It didn’t pander to their interests. This was a campaign of fifty thousand people who volunteered, and canvassed, and made calls. Last week a lot of people who had been feeling powerless realized that they still have some power in this country. And that’s a start. Let’s just hope a lot more people are learning from that.”

caption: When I started Humans of New York I had only been photographing for three months. I had no idea what I was doing. But I was bailed out by the explosion of social media, sheer determination, and the power of a good idea. I was a twenty-six-year-old kid with this crazy dream to tell the story of New York City, one person at a time. And it worked. The first Humans of New York book sold almost a million copies— but even then, I was only beginning to figure out the craft. In the twelve years since I have learned so much: about photography, about interviewing, about writing, about people. And I was moved by the urge to do it again. I wanted to try my best to capture this city; only this time, I knew exactly what I was doing. For nearly two years I took a step back from social media. I focused on one thing: this book. I collected hundreds of stories from all over this city, with the hope that Dear New York would become the most enduring piece of this crazy idea I had, all those years ago. In all the madness and joy of what’s happening at Grand Central this week, I want to pause for a moment to honor and introduce the book that inspired it all. Dear New York is based on a simple idea: This city is humanity itself. Every type of person is here: every ethnicity, every culture, every belief, every viewpoint. And all of us are crammed onto the same narrow sidewalks, packed into the same subway cars. We sometimes annoy the hell out of each other, but we also show up for each other. We take care of each other. In a world that can seem to be teetering on the edge, New York remains something to celebrate. Humanity remains something to celebrate. Dear New York is published today. It was made with all my heart, and I very much hope that you love it.

caption: “When I was fifteen I lost a younger brother to a guy who raped and killed him, and I took the law into my own hands. I don’t want to say much more to that effect, but when it happened, I lost faith in humanity. I didn’t trust anybody. Life became all about me, so I just survived. A lot of my family members still won’t talk to me because they remember a Johnny that wasn’t trustworthy. I became a wanderer, there’s no better way to say it. And one day ten years ago I wandered into this park looking for a place to sit down. I saw an old man playing chess, in exchange for donations. He was waiting for an oncomer so I came on. He beat me senseless. But it was my first taste of communication with a stranger sitting across from me. And I thought to myself: ‘I can do that too.’ I bought myself a chess board. In the beginning I got the shit kicked out of me by strangers from all over the world. But I grew game after game, learning the fundamentals, then learning all the other stuff. And now I teach them to anybody who wants to play. I get donations, but it’s not the money that’s the fruit of my take. It’s when people sit down. I call it fruit, is that weird? Because when you share an activity with someone for fifteen minutes, a half hour—it nourishes your soul. Me looking at you, us laughing, doing bad moves, good moves— it’s all so nourishing. Because of chess I got to witness the difference between good and evil. So many have sat across from me that are so good— honest people with great, great hearts. I knew that very first day that this seat would make my life more significant. I knew as long as I kept sitting here, people would keep coming. And there is so much fruit that you get from people. Not all the people, can’t go that far. There are some around here that I would like to strangle, I’m not shitting. But we maintain. Because look, I’ve got problems too. And I’m not looking to blow the house down.”

caption:
I chose to make this video because Dear NY was genuinely one of the most beautiful and impressive things I’ve seen in the city. @humansofny pulled off something I didn’t think was possible. To put its scale in perspective:

- The MET sees about ~5.7M visitors per year
- MoMA about ~2.7M annual visitors 
- Statue of Liberty ~4.2M annual visitors 

And Dear New York passed them all in foot traffic, in less than two weeks!

Props to Brandon and the team for creating a moment that’ll live on in New York’s history.

caption: How does a two-week art installation about community grow into something like this? I think it’s because people are tired of ‘connecting’ through screens. Nobody wants to live in a metaverse, whatever the hell that is. We don’t want to become passive consumers of songs that ‘seem’ human, art that ‘seems’ human, friends that ‘seem’ human. None of this stuff is what we need. We need to create. We need to connect. We need to serve other people if we’re going to have any sort of place or belonging in this world. If humanity is going to thrive— and if art is going to thrive – there is only one place for it to go: the real world. Dear New York was founded upon the increasingly rare belief that humanity is pretty freaking amazing. This isn’t a perfect world. Every day the media brings us new examples of glaring injustice and senseless violence. We still have much work to do. But while we do the work, let us not forget how much love there is in this world. In New York City alone, in a single day, there are millions of stories of people taking care of each other. These stories don’t make the evening news, but they’re no less real. And when you sum it all up—the good and the bad – humanity is still worth fighting for. It’s still something to celebrate. Dear New York will close tomorrow at 8 pm, with a short choral performance by hundreds of children from @ypcofnyc .

caption: “There was a bad break up, sort of. It was eight months ago. I’m past it now. But I had to experience that for the first time. I don’t think I handled it as well as I could. At the time I couldn’t grasp that maybe it wasn’t anybody’s fault. Maybe I just wanted to be with the person for longer than they wanted to be with me. But accepting things that you don’t want to happen is really, really hard. It’s like: ‘Why do they get to walk around, and keep living their life, while I’m miserable all the time?’ It didn’t seem fair. So I might have reacted in a way that was disproportionate, to make the person feel more guilty than they needed to. Sometimes that’s your only recourse when someone hurts you: feeling aggrieved, and making it known. Not that it keeps you from suffering. But there is a sense of power in it. It allows you to redistribute the pain that you’re feeling. You can make their life a hassle for a bit, hurt their feelings, tell everyone they’re a big asshole. When the truth is: maybe they were just living their life, trying their best, and you got hurt. There’s not always a villain. Sometimes you just get fucked up by somebody exercising their own autonomy.”

caption:
A few months ago I got an unfortunate update that Little Humans was going out of print. It was a sad news to receive, because while not exactly a ‘money maker,’ Little Humans had a special place in our family’s heart. I’d written it over twelve years ago. My publisher asked me to write a kids’ book, and I told them: ‘Of course!’ I didn’t have any children at the time, but I thought: ‘How hard could it be?’ It turned out to be much harder than I’d imagined. After several failed attempts I was pushing up against my deadline, so I recruited the help of my girlfriend who had a lot of babysitting experience. We took an overnight trip to Vermont, sat on the floor of a cozy cabin, wrote a little ode to being a kid, and paired it with some of the ‘most fun’ kid portraits from Humans of New York. We were super proud of it. 
 
But it didn’t exactly set the children’s book market on fire. It was listed for ages 4 to 8, but it soon apparent that it was far too simplistic for that age group. Whoops! But a funny thing started to happen. Over the years I began getting emails saying: ‘my toddler is obsessed with Little Humans.’ Our friends began having kids and would send us ‘Nest’ recordings of their toddlers ‘reading’ Little Humans in their cribs, over and over. My girlfriend became my wife, we had three kids of our own, and the pattern was confirmed. The littlest kids love Little Humans. They love seeing pictures of all different kinds of kids, and the words are easy to memorize, so they love to ‘read along.’ 
 
I’d always regretted that we hadn’t made Little Humans as a ‘board book’ aimed at the youngest children. And when we learned it was going out of print, we were sad. But the book angels smiled down on Little Humans. The fine folks at Farrar, Strauss, and Giroux agreed to rescue it from oblivion and re-issue a small run of Little Humans board books—for babies and toddlers. If you’re looking for a fun, engaging way to introduce your little human to all the different types of kids in this world, the Little Human Board Book is out today. Long live Little Humans! caption: A few years ago I received a DM from @zohrankmamdani. Only recently did I discover its existence. It was a very unusual DM—especially coming from a local assemblyman who would soon be running for higher office. He had very little name recognition at the time, and could have benefited from publicity. But unlike the thousands of messages I’ve received from people with something to promote, Zohran did not ask to be featured on Humans of New York. Instead he asked if he could introduce me to taxi drivers that were struggling beneath the burden of debt. Coming from a man with political ambitions, this self-denying request was so strange as to be almost singular. I don’t endorse politicians on Humans of New York. But I’ll endorse a good man. And it was a good man who cleared 30 minutes from his schedule yesterday to swing by Grand Central to visit Dear New York. Nearly fifty student artists were visiting that day with their families, and I thought a surprise visit from this widely-loved future mayor would be a special memory for all of them. Before Zohran’s arrival I was convinced I’d made a terrible mistake. The Vanderbilt Hall exhibit was filled to capacity with adult visitors. Dear New York is self-funded so there was very little staff and security for crowd control. In the crush of people I was almost certain this special day for the kids would devolve into thirty minutes of selfie requests. But everyone rose to the occasion. Hundreds of adults quickly cleared the room and stood outside the exhibit. Eleven very notable adult artists are also featured in the exhibition, but even they took a step back, so that these students could briefly have the stage to themselves. Each child stood by their work and Zohran was able to meet all of them, one at a time, and honor their contributions to the most-visited art show in New York City. Thanks to everyone who ceded the stage yesterday to make this moment possible. Thank you Zohran for literally sitting down on the floor so that these young artists could feel so tall. Thank you for continually centering other people in your life and work. And thank you, for being such an important part of Dear New York.

caption: “I thought he was a gay at first. I’d been looking for an artist to paint a canvas in my living room, and Mitya was a friend of my roommate. So I hired him. He showed up in his tight pants, and he painted the most beautiful mural showing women of all colors supporting each other. I was attracted to him, I liked his accent. But I thought: ‘Definitely gay.’ And I’m 64 years old. I hadn’t dated in eight years. I didn’t know how to kiss, nothing. So I wasn’t exactly looking to meet someone. But two months later my roommate moves out, and she tells me that Mitya is looking for place to stay. He seemed harmless enough, so I said OK.  We had a party when he moved in. My daughter has a lot of gay friends, and I told them to go casually talk to him. They reported back to me: ‘Not gay, just European.’ And everything happened organically from there. We went to a museum one afternoon. Then a few nights later we were watching a movie and things got physical. We’ve been together for two years now. He’s so attentive to me. He does all the cooking. I haven’t had anyone taking care of me like this for many, many years. The males in my life didn’t show up in a positive way. I grew up around a lot of single women who carried the torch themselves, so I have trust issues with men. But I feel safe with Mitya. Make no mistake, he can be a difficult person. He can be extremely stubborn. He gets in these artists moods. But the Mitya you see is the Mitya you get. I’m a realist. I know this is a temporary relationship. I’m twenty years older than him. I’ve told him that if he would like to engage with someone else, he can. As long as he comes to me first. He gets annoyed when I talk like this. He says: ‘We are in the here and now.’ But I don’t want him staying with me forever. Mitya deserves a family. He’d be such a good husband, a great dad. And I can’t give him that. Maybe we’ll meet at another time, in another life, when we’re closer in age. I think God brought us together for a reason. Mitya gave me the full experience of what a man should stand for. Being with him was like being in a cocoon. I’ll have to leave one day, but I’ll have become a butterfly.” @mityapisliak

caption: “I was nineteen when we started dating. He was older, owned three companies, had all this life experience. By the time I saw his true colors it was too late; he’d moved me away from home and put me through every form of abuse you can imagine. When I finally told him I was leaving, he got violent. It left me half-deaf and disabled. But I escaped and went to live with my parents. For two years I wouldn’t leave the house; I was too afraid of him coming back. Dad did everything he could to coax me out of it. First it was simple things: ‘Why don’t you read a book? Why don’t you come sit on the couch?’ He’d been in the Marines, so he’d tell me about his own struggles with PTSD. Eventually he got me out on the front porch. Then he got me playing basketball. Then he got me into therapy, and he’d drive me to and from. My first job was at my parents’ vet. It was just an hour at a time, watching over the boarded dogs. But I liked it, I felt safe. My boss would tell me: this dog got rescued, it’s been abused, it’s head shy. And I’d think: I know that feeling. For my birthday in 2014, Dad loaned me the money to put down a deposit on a mobile grooming van. It was one year after my daughter was born; Dad would pick her up from daycare so I could go to work. I paid him back in three years. Things were going great, my daughter and I had our own apartment. But last year Mom went into the ICU and I had to stop working for months to take care of her. Then the generator on the van broke— costs more to fix than to replace— and I can’t afford it. I’m back living with Dad again. I don’t want to stay in his house and live off his retirement. My daughter is thirteen, she needs her own space. She’s acting out at school. I feel like I’m failing as a mom, failing completely. Dad will bring me out to cut grass with him. He’ll be like: ‘Hey kiddo, what’s going on? I know the van’s down, you’re stressing, but you still have to be here for your daughter.’ Last week I told him: ‘Dad, I’m done.’ He said: ‘If you say that again, I’ll smack you. Look back at what you’ve conquered. You’ve already come through the worst part of your life. You’re not giving up now. You’re like me. We’re never done.”

caption: “I nurtured two independent young minds, and then I bore the brunt of that independence. I think every parent goes through the same thing. In order for us to stop controlling them, they have to break away. It’s programmed in their DNA. They need to hate us a little in order to develop their own identity. My youngest called me ‘Stage Mom’ once. She immediately apologized. But that one hurt, because it implies control. And it’s never been about control for me. It’s just enthusiasm: I have all this knowledge, somebody passed it on to me, and I want to pass it on to someone else. But when you’re Mom, it’s impossible for your opinions to not come across as judgment. So I’m learning to shut up. I’m trying to stop saying obvious things that she already knows. Sometimes I still do, but she’s learning to not aggressively respond. She’ll just say: ‘Yes, yes, yes.’ And when I hear that, I know she’s telling me to shut up. So we’re learning each other. Right now she’s studying acting at NYU. I’m visiting from LA, and we got to hang out in her dorm last night. She’s recovering from a concussion, so two of her friends cooked dinner. I got to see how they appreciate each other. The three of them just finished collaborating on a film. They entered it into a film festival, and my daughter won the best actor award. They’re creating these things and growing together and I had nothing to do with any of it. But still, they chose to include me. We were four equals that night. We were talking film all the time, exchanging our ideas and stuff. I got to sleep in a dorm! Only because I had to drive her to the doctor in the morning, but still— how cool is that? When a super cool group of people from a younger generation want to include you— there’s no better compliment. It felt like the end of being the parent, and maybe an inkling of what it’s like to be included in a different way. As more of an equal, a friend. She’s only 20. I’m hoping there will be more opportunities before I get too old and annoying. Or more annoying, in different ways. I just got the text that they want to hang out with me tonight again. So I mean, c’mon. That’s a win. That’s a win, win, win!”

caption: “Everyone has their problems. And my mom, you know, had a drinking problem. She wasn’t a perfect lady. But she loved a lot. And when I lost her, I lost me. It was Christmas Eve. My Uncle Rome and Uncle Albert sat me down and said: ‘Your moms got hit by a car.’ A car hit her and dragged her down the hill, it took her away on Christmas Eve. It was bad for me. I broke all the windows in the apartment. I threw the chairs; I went in a terrible rage, very terrible. I went down, downhill. It was a hard life. It was a hard life like rats. School wasn’t good for me. I couldn’t comprehend, I couldn’t catch up. Everything I had, it was taken. They’d call me all types of names. I was just a kid. Like why would ya’ll say that to me? When I came home I just locked myself in my room. There were pictures on the wall, pictures of my moms. So I was like: I ain’t gonna leave my room. And that wasn’t good. I was like an animal in a cage. I allowed the demons to come into play. They tricked my mind. They told me you don’t need God. You don’t need him, you need us.  It’s OK to do bad things. It’s OK to sell drugs. When you lose somebody you love, man, it hurts. I walk the world with feelings, and sometimes I crash inside my soul. Sometimes I debate with my soul. It can happen that way, where you and your soul have a conversation. It’s like, yo, what we doing here? Why do we even exist? I go back to being a kid, feeling like I ain’t worth nothing. And that’s why I stay spider. Deshawn and the spider became as one, an entity that can’t be broken. It’s kind of hard to explain, but the spider and me, we love each other. He’s my best friend. Sometimes there’s a disagreement. Sometimes there’s a debate between Deshawn and the spider. I feel like I’m letting Deshawn down by becoming the spider. Sometimes he feels left out. Like the spider became more than Deshawn. Like the spider took over. He says that it’s not good to overshadow the person that was there before this fight even came into his life. And I don’t want him to feel that way. Like he’s dying. I don’t like to use that word, but sometimes I feel like I’m making Deshawn die. To become a spider.”

caption: A MESSAGE FROM ANGEL: In the middle of the chaos there was a miracle. Having been cheated, no money, not sleeping, and all of this stress—I was preparing myself for anything. But part of me was still having hope, that if I could not be affected by all this, and somehow keep my essence, then perhaps the chaos might transform into something beautiful. Eventually the burden grew so heavy that I could not continue, so I asked for help. I started speaking with customers: reaching out to share my misery, my gratefulness, my everything. That was the beginning— letting go. People started organizing to help out of this situation in any way possible. Thank you to everyone involved in this fundraiser. Thank you to all the people working here, all the suppliers, thank you to the musicians who come here and share their music, thank you to all the customers—everyone coming to Caravan of Dreams is a potential friend. When I start reading comments from people, all the understanding, all the gratitude, all the love and support I was feeling makes me cry. I should even say to the people who cheated me, I learned something from you and I am developing more unconditional love. I do not justify the negativity but unfortunately we must sometimes suffer many times in order to improve our behaviors, and change the negative into the positive. If there is anyone from the last 35 years that I have not remembered, all of you are in my heart. I would like to conclude with the word ‘desire.’ A wise man teaching about the invisible once said that everything starts from a desire. When I was a young man I had a desire to be a good person, and that was the beginning of getting more. Afterwards came words like faith, humility, gratitude. Then 35 years ago I had the desire to start a restaurant with plant-based, organic, clean food, made with love, with good intention. And this became Caravan of Dreams. The great vibrations that we generate when our desires are positive—these miracles are the result. What happened lately, with so many people giving abundance, little money here and there, making big, beautiful things for Caravan of Dreams. This is a miracle. Thank you to everyone. I love everyone.

caption: “Every time I finished, the first thought was: I want to get out of here. I don’t know how to describe the feeling: whatever is the opposite of integrity. I was conniving, cheating, lying to others, lying to myself. Sex can take over your whole life. I taught writing out of college and then I threw it all away. I worked odd jobs so I could be a night person and do whatever I wanted. I was never honest in a relationship, never monogamous. It was exhausting always trying to cover my tracks. Forget the possibility of STD’s. How do you build integrity if you’re engaging in those behaviors: calling all these girls, juggling all these women? That’s why I drank on top of it. So I could lie to myself: ‘At least it’s just a prostitute. At least I’m not having an affair.’ Those were some of the stories I‘d tell myself so I could pretend to like myself. But eventually it got to a point where it was just too much. For the first time I decided to see a therapist, and it was the therapist who recommended the meetings. If you tell people you’re in AA, they say ‘Good job.’ But there’s still a lot of shame with this disease. So people are doing this stuff in the dark. Especially porn. Which for a long time I thought was the solution to my addiction, but I realize now it was the root. I met my current wife not long after I started the program. It’s been over ten years, and it’s the first relationship where I’ve never cheated. Never, never, never. I’ve only told her two lies the entire relationship. I lied about my age on the dating app profile, but I confessed to that on our first date. And I lied about having a hemorrhoid. I didn’t want to tell her, so I said it was some other shit. Other than that, we have zero secrets. You couldn’t touch my phone before because I’d be too afraid of what you’d see, but my phone is an open book now. It’s so corny, but honesty really is the best policy. Now if you ask me what I did last night—I don’t have to even think. It’s so much easier. And I’m trying to instill the same thing in my kids. We don’t lie in our house. My kids know that their father doesn’t lie. And when my daughter gives a pinky promise— that shit is like gold.”

caption: “About the time I retired I came up with five goals. I have the list on my phone. And the first goal is simply to be with my wife in every respect: physically, emotionally, as a lover, as a supporter—I want that to be the focal point of my life. Because after 26 years of marriage, I’m still very much in love. I still very much enjoy who she is. She’s wonderful to her friends and community. She has the most amazing big smile; it comes out every time she hears a piece of exciting news or a salacious piece of gossip. She’s really smart. Not smart the way I am: I was a museum curator, I’m into nuclear physics, molecular biology. But she’s wiser and a good observer and a good listener. I tend to get carried away with worries and concerns; I suffer from long-term, treatment-resistant depression. It’s been 43 different medications including convulsive shock therapy. But she’s sustained me through it all. She always knows how to bring me back to earth. She’ll provide a perspective that is otherwise absent. She’s makes sure I get what I need—even if it’s just keeping me fed. So during this chapter I want to care for her very intentionally, and I’m still figuring out what that should look like. It’s a lifetime of work to maintain and nourish our connections, because things shift. Things happen, people get sick. Two years ago she was diagnosed with a rare and deadly form of eye cancer. caption: “He’s never liked the word ‘girlfriend’ so we settled on ‘soulmate.’ I’m a journalist, I’m very logical. But Angel is the opposite. He has this childlike faith that everything is going to work out, and it opens doors to miracles. How else can you explain this place? A vegan restaurant run by a completely irrational man, surviving for 35 years in the heart of Manhattan. Even in the good years the restaurant barely made money, because Angel only cares about having the purest and highest of everything. He imports all his olive oil from one region in Morocco. Not for taste—it’s more bitter— but because it has the most polyphenols. He puts $90 probiotics in his mango shakes, and people don’t even know they’re in there. He serves the cleanest water in the city; he filters it seven times. He makes his own table cleaner! None of this makes any business sense, but Angel has no aspirations for material goods. You’d be shocked if you saw his apartment: it’s the tiniest room. He drives an old car from 1966. Before the pandemic the restaurant was very busy; we had to call ahead before we came. But so many regulars left town, and now there are nights with only two or three customers. On those nights I look at him and he looks ten years older: his posture, the light in his eyes. Recently he was taken advantage of by someone offering to invest his money. The man was recommended by a rabbi. So Angel scraped together everything he had. I told him it wasn’t a good idea—but Angel is innocent. When a person says they believe in God, or the Universe, he can find no darkness in them. Angel lost everything, $300,000. He’s running the restaurant on credit now. The debt scares me more than anything. Angel is 76, and I hate to see him taking on so much debt at the end of his life. Every day he stays open, he falls further behind. But he won’t close the doors because Caravan of Dreams has never been a business to him. It’s a spiritual mission. Angel believes in his heart that Caravan of Dreams is contributing to a brighter future for the world. And if he doesn’t keep it open, the world will lose that future. He won’t let go. He’s driven by faith. He thinks all he has to do is believe.”

caption: “All advertising directed at women says: ‘You’re not good enough.’ With men it’s a little different. The message is: ‘You’re great, but you can be even greater.’ That’s why I’m always going to have a chip on my shoulder against capitalism. There’s this scarcity mentality: eighteen people have all the money, and there isn’t enough to go around, so the rest of us have to compete with each other for scraps. The whole thing is based on this idea of competing with your fellow man. It’s one of the big reasons I created The Free Store. To show that there’s this undercurrent of kindness and camaraderie that also motivates people, and it has nothing to do with competition. I opened the first location during the height of the pandemic; things were really dark. Everyone was leaving New York and going back to Ohio or Connecticut or wherever the fuck they’re from, and they’re just leaving their belongings on the street. All this valuable stuff, just sitting on the street. It’s like: ‘What the fuck?’ So I hung up some shelves on one of these boarded-up buildings, stocked them with perfectly good stuff from the street, and hung up a sign that said: ‘Free Store.’ I ended up opening seventeen locations. I’m proud of it, I’m very proud of it. The Free Store had no owners, no managers, no customers. Only participants. Just people being people. There were a few motherfuckers, but almost everyone took only what they needed. Nobody was guarding these shelves, and for the most part they were always stacked with good stuff. I think it challenged this whole scarcity mindset, and it proved that even in the darkest times we will always have enough. It’s been my experience that when people see just how much stuff there is, the less likely they are to hoard everything. And the more faith they’ll have in, like, their fellow man.”

caption: “I love him, but he was a very tough dad. He was something called a txiv geej; it’s a very respected position in our culture. At funerals he would play an instrument called a geej; it looks like a long flute with six smaller flutes attached. And its song is supposed to help the spirit pass on to the next world. My dad wanted nothing more than for his sons to continue the tradition. He’d make us practice for hours every day. When we were kids it was kinda cool. We’d play at Hmong New Year celebrations, and everyone would watch, and they’d be very polite. But as we became teenagers, it was like—this is not cool. We were living in a small town in Wisconsin— not a lot of Asian folks in general. I was focused on trying to get by every day. I just wanted to hang out. I guess you could say I became more American. We had so many arguments over it, there was a lot of: ‘I don’t understand. This isn’t why we brought you to the States, not for this.’ I was very hurt by it; obviously you want your dad to be proud of you. But he was very hurt by it too—that he didn’t have a son who was observing the religion, playing the instrument, following his footsteps. It might sound like he was being selfish, but I think it was more selfless than selfish. He thought that if I didn’t follow the religion—our spirits would go two different places. It’s what he truly believed. And he wanted me to follow his footsteps after death as well. But toward the end of his life, he finally told me: ‘You’re a dad now. You’ve become your own man, and I respect whatever path you choose to follow.’ And I was so thankful for that. At his funeral one of his best friends played the geej. My father left a recording of exactly how he wanted it played; it’s almost as if he was providing the exact coordinates of where he wanted his soul to be.”

caption: “My mother had a lot of different men in and out. People would come live with us. We were always moving around. I counted the places we lived at one point, and it was over twenty-five. It was chaos, emotional chaos. The not knowing where you’re going to live, not knowing if you’re going to be able to eat. Not knowing clearly what the fuck is actually going on. I moved out and got my own apartment when I turned sixteen. Went to Job Corps, finished Job Corps. Got my GED. By the time I was seventeen I was living by myself, going to college, I had a job. I was meeting a lot of people I would otherwise have never met. I’m proud of myself. I’m living up to my own standard. I made it through all this bullshit. I had enough power to do it. I had enough talent to do it. I felt like a super independent woman. There’s a joy of doing things on your own: the freedom, the not having to answer to anyone. Nobody you have to call and say: ‘Hey, it’s me. This is where I’m going, this is what I’m doing, this is when I’m going to be home.’ There’s also a pain of doing it on your own—and it happens to be that exact same thing.”

caption: “I didn’t talk to my father for twenty-five years. My therapist told me: if you’re in a relationship where you’re always giving, and the other person is always taking—just drop your end of the log. Stop reaching out and see if the other person picks it up. I was always scared to do that with my dad because I was afraid he wouldn’t, and that’s exactly what happened. So I cut him off. The silent treatment made me feel powerful because I could control it. People tried to warn me: ‘It’s more your burden than his.’ For the longest time I didn’t believe them, but it was true. It required so much energy standing my ground, never taking his calls. I was still hanging onto the anger and rage. He’d been an alcoholic my entire life. I never felt supported. I never felt like he was interested in what I was doing. I never felt like I got love from him. And I needed some recognition of that. I thought if I engaged with him, I’d be letting him off the hook. I’m not sure when things changed. Have you ever had a moment where you just decide you don’t want to be dependent on someone anymore? I’ve had it with past boyfriends, and one day it just happened with my father too. It was right after my husband had a stroke. I knew my father had recently had a stroke too, so on the drive home from the hospital I gave him a call. We talk occasionally now. I don’t demand anything of him. I don’t try to change him. I know we’re never going to have the kind of relationship that I always wanted, but I get that from other people. I have a big life. There are people who care about me, who I love, and I know they love me. And I think he loves me in his own way, I guess. He’s had a rough go of it: his dad committed suicide when he was eight. So he does the best he can. I always used to say: “Well, that’s not good enough!” But I’ve let go of that. I saw him for the first time in twenty-five years at my niece’s wedding. He’s a little old man now. Eighty-two, and a little hunched. My sisters were there. We all danced. Everyone was laughing, catching up. There was no fighting. There was no: “When I was six years old, you didn’t do my laundry!” I don’t know how to describe it; it was just light.”

caption: “My mom was super against it. She was like: ‘Don’t go. You don’t need to do this.’ But I was convinced it was the one thing that would finally make me happy. I’ve believed that since I was a kid. I used to stretch for like an hour a day, hoping to grow. Then when I was sixteen I found out about a procedure in India called limb-lengthening. I said to my mom: that’s exactly what I’m going to do, and my mind has been set on it for ten years. I moved back home, started working sales jobs, saving for the operation. The procedure was $60,000. Some people go to Turkey; I went to Europe. The day of the operation I was scared as shit, I won’t lie. They’re shaving my legs, it’s like: fuck, this feels real. They broke both my femurs and inserted an expandable rod. Some people grow five to six inches; I added three. At first I was happy with what I saw in the mirror. I finally felt like I was enough. But the recovery took months; I was all alone, in a foreign country. And the feelings of emptiness came back. I’ve had these depressive episodes my entire life. I’ve never understood them. My life is good: I have a family, I have a house. But it always felt like something was missing. I thought for sure it was my height, but I’m realizing now it was much deeper than that. I love my Mom. But she was a single mom; she’s very old school. And I don’t think she gave me the emotional support I needed during childhood. Nothing I did was ever enough. If I ever needed to talk about something, she’d say: ‘It’s not that serious.’ She was always working. I had to manage everything alone, and that’s overwhelming for a kid. I’m trying to be compassionate with myself. What’s done is done. And if I hadn’t done it, I don’t think I’d have come to this conclusion. I was reading about this a couple days ago; some people don’t realize until their 40’s or 50’s that there’s an underlying emptiness and nothing external is going to fill it. It would have required something drastic happening to me later in life. It can be easy to remember things that happened in childhood. It’s much harder to remember the things that didn’t happen. And it was the things that didn’t happen that kind of fucked me up.”

caption: “I’m 66 now. I’m looking at the end of this journey and I don’t have time for bullshit. We are mission-specific here, no fluff. The life expectancy for kids in this community is a decade less than my own kids’. And it’s a very unhealthy, medically-induced life. It’s a function of the environment; in this neighborhood there are twenty-nine pharmacies, fifty-five fast food restaurants, and not a single supermarket. But environment can be changed. I started Harlem Grown fourteen years ago by turning an abandoned junkyard into an urban farm— just to give kids a safe space and teach them about nutrition. But things started happening on the periphery: the kids’ parents would come hang out, and sometimes I’d send them home with fresh food from the farm: a few herbs, some tomatoes. I thought it was cute at first, but people heard we were giving out food and started showing up. Since then we’ve just kept ramping up. We have fourteen farms now. We’ve tried to stay true to our niche of providing fresh, nutritious, healthy foods: fruits and vegetables in particular. With the help of our partners, last year we were able to give away 160,000 pounds of food. I can regurgitate this shit, but when we get to the personal points man, it just fucks me up. Twenty-three kids from our program became the first in their family to attend four-year colleges. The first girl who ever joined our program is pursuing her PhD. Where would she be without that intervention? That’s my terror. Imagine if we weren’t here, how worse it would be for so many. When I started this, I was just looking for a volunteer opportunity. In my mind I was killing time while figuring out my next move. But the kids became my next move. You meet these kids, and you learn about their lives, and what are you supposed to do? When you don’t know about something— you can claim you just don’t know. But once you do know, what do you do? Harlem Grown grew from one tiny, little lot that we called a farm to something that has been able to create so much joy and opportunity. It wasn’t money that did that. It was time. I had time, and we all have time. But time for what? And that’s what we have to ask ourselves.”

caption: “We were driving to Atlanta to see my parents when I got a text from their mother. It said: ‘I moved to Chicago.’ When we got back to New York, her stuff was gone. We’d been going through a rough patch, but in my opinion—nothing that couldn’t be fixed. No infidelity or anything like that. She’s an artist too. I guess she’s on a journey to find herself. My parents offered to take the kids in Georgia, so that option was on the table. But I thought: ‘Imagine what their life will be like if they lose both of you.’ The first month was rough. Catastrophic. But I took a step back. I thought: ‘You still have the kids. She’s not contesting. A lot of people don’t have family, so start there. And don’t squander what you have.’ Before COVID I’d been the manager of a huge market: a whole bunch of people. And I didn’t love them, so I figured managing four kids would be easier than that. As a manager I learned to ask my employees to communicate what they’re going to do. Ask them what part they’re going to play. And if they understand what happens if they don’t do their part. So I did the same thing with the kids. It ended up becoming a collective project. My role is to make sure that we’re not out in the street, the lights are on, and we have food in the fridge. Everyone cleans. Everyone does their schoolwork. Libby helps with the twins’ hair. My son handles the garbage and the heavier things. The twins need to listen to their big sister. It’s a whole checks and balances thing. They never embarrass me when I take them places. Not because they’re worried about losing things, but because I taught them that they represent me. We’ve made it three years now. I felt happy on New Years; it’s just a reminder— we pushed through another year.’ My goal is to get them through these next six years with as little harm as possible. They have their own dreams: Libby wants to be an artist, my son is a musician, one of the twins wants to be a train engineer, the other wants to go into the medical field. I never want them to say: ‘We could have done this, but Mom left.’ So that’s my goal: for them to be able to do all those things, despite our challenges. That’s the reason I’m going so hard.”

caption: “We stayed together for two years and realized that we were probably better off as friends than as a couple. Our daughter was two at the time. It was horrible. One day you have access to your child 24/7, and it’s all you’ve known. Then the next day it’s split in half and it’s not always controlled by you. You’re living across the street, but you’re still trying to be the protector. I just didn’t want any trauma. That was the big thing for me: no trauma. Because I grew up with it. I never wanted her emotionally needing me, crying herself to sleep: ‘Daddy, daddy, daddy.’ And to my knowledge she never has. For me it was about consistency: always showing up, never being late. And staying friends with her mother. That was very important to me. After the initial split I remember it was about sixty weeks in a row of me suggesting to my ex: let’s all go to dinner, let’s all go to dinner. Finally she said yes, and it’s become something we’ve done regularly for the past ten years. Our daughter is twelve now, and we all had dinner the other night. We talked about what’s going on at school. We joked about things. I like to think from the outside we looked like any nuclear family out to dinner. I just think it’s so important for our daughter to consistently see the two of us, being our natural selves, in the presence of each other. I’m not the perfect father. And she’s not the perfect mother. We have different parenting styles, and we disagree on a lot of things. But I don’t think we’ve ever been jerks to each other. My ex would always cover for me if I travelled, and I travel a lot, because I work for a Swedish paper mill. I know it was hard for her a lot of times. But if she asked me to cover a weekend, even if I had other plans, I’d agree. And we’ve never used access as a weapon. Even if we were in the middle of a disagreement—we both had access to our daughter every day. We would never say: ‘This isn’t your day’ or ‘This isn’t your week.’ Technically it’s not my week right now, but I’m on the way to pick up my daughter from school. I’m going to take her for a quick snack, and then I’m going to drop her off at her mom’s.”

caption: “Ten years ago I met a professional flower girl. She was 24-years old. She was going through a tough time, so my husband and I tried to help her. We let her use this space. We laid out all the money: transportation, allowance, everything. I worked alongside her in the shop. But the flower girl, she always party. She took the $3,000 I gave her and disappeared. It’s OK. She was young, whatever. We were going to close the shop, but my husband said: ‘You are always happy when you are here, why don’t you run it yourself?’ So that’s what I did. I used to be a fashion designer, so I’m very good with color. I know composition naturally. And also— everything I touch, it grows. People think it’s a miracle. It’s not a miracle. It’s just a matter of caring. When your customer authorizes you to do something, do the best you can offer. People are not dumb. They can see how much thought and time you put into your work. They can tell if you are like crocodile, doing as little as possible, trying to eat all the money you can. Look at all the shops up and down the street—you can see who puts their heart into it. Look at the plants in front of the store. If the plants are dying, the business is dying. It’s a matter of caring. You must care for everything around you. First, I take care of myself. That is most important. I’m seventy-one. If my muscles feel pain, I stop. I’ll do my stretching. Then I care for my husband. He’s a very good partner. Two years ago he had a stroke; he has some minor health things still. So I care for him. We adopted two little kitties. We make them delicious food like human food: turkey, chicken, fish. They grow very big. We take good care of them. Then we care for our friends, our customers, even our customer’s dogs. If you treat your customers’ dogs well, they will smell you and remember you. Everything is together: plants, animals, humans. If you care, you will grow. But not enough people care. It’s not that they aren’t smart. It’s that they want to try everything, so they never care enough about any one thing. Too many choices. Me? This is my only choice. Come by anytime, I’m around.”

caption: “I’m feeling a sense of being completely blindsided by the issues of the world because everything was working out for me. In our political philosophy class we’re learning about this guy, John Rawls. And he talks about how whether you’re rich or poor, and even really if you’re talented or talentless—it has nothing to do with you. It’s arbitrary. So much of your life is shaped by the position you’re born into. And I happen to have had a really lucky roll of the dice. I had, like, great parents. I lived in an apartment on the Upper West Side. I went to a private school where I got to call my teachers by their first names. I had wonderful friends, cute dogs, nice vacations. I had the greatest roll of the dice ever. Yet I walk five paces outside of my front door, and I’ll see someone who had a shit roll: sleeping on the streets, just trying to survive. It’s like: what did I do to deserve this? Nothing. I could easily just fade into the background and do whatever is great for myself and my family. I don’t think anyone would notice, or blame me. Not everyone needs to change the world. My girlfriend didn’t have as much privilege as me, and she is very focused on her dream of owning a house. I think that’s wonderful. I hope she accomplishes that, and I can live with her in that house one day. But I’ve lived in a house. I’ve lived a lavish life. I’ve had a lot of pleasure, I’ve had a lot of joy. I don’t need to constantly pursue that, you know. I’d love to try my best to use this ‘everything working out for me’ to do something for someone else.”

caption: “I’ve been on forty first dates over the course of three years. And that’s not counting the hundred conversations on dating apps that didn’t go anywhere. So yeah— I thought meeting someone would be a little easier than this. Maybe the city is just a difficult place to date, or maybe it’s just how the apps are designed, but it’s a pretty cold environment, pretty emotionless. People don’t seem to put much emotion into the way they put themselves out there. There’s a lot of ghosting. It happens most often before you even get to the date. You’ll be trying to set something up, and the person falls off. But there are times when the date does happen, and you’ll think it went well, but when you follow up a few days later there’s no response. People seem to have this mentality that if they’ve just met someone online, they don’t owe them anything. And I agree with that to some extent. But I think you owe people the common decency to reject them. I don’t think it’s difficult to say: ‘I’m not interested.’ One time I’d been dating someone for a month-and-a-half. We’d just spent a weekend together in New Jersey, but when I texted him the next day he didn’t respond ever again. Maybe I’m just too sensitive. A lot of people seem to be able to say: ‘If the person ghosted me, then they weren’t for me.’ But I end up feeling like I’m not interesting enough, or that there’s something missing with me that people can sense, and that’s why it never goes anywhere deeper. Maybe that’s my low self-esteem coming out. Maybe if I had higher self-esteem I wouldn’t take ghosting so badly. I’m still only 27, but I’m losing hope of actually finding someone. I’m so fed up with the interactions I’m having that I don’t want to put myself out there as much. People keep disappointing me. So it’s like: ‘Is it really worth my peace to keep interacting with people?’ But I feel like I have to keep doing it. Because if I stop, then I’ll get into this head space where I don’t want to put myself out there again.’”

caption: “I was a happy child from about five to seven. That’s when we got taken from our mother and sent to live with our aunt. I remember waking up on Christmas, snow on the ground, my uncle outside hanging up lights. Beautiful memories. But at one point it all stopped, and after that I just remember screaming. My uncle would scare me to the point where I’d piss myself. He was never satisfied until that happened. My aunt tried to stand up for me. Whenever my uncle said: ‘That’s not my son,’ she’d tell him: ‘We decided to do this.’ But eventually he stopped loving her too and after that the hatred was coming from everywhere. I tried to suicide myself before I knew what suicide was. But I made it through. I’ve been on my own now since the age of nineteen and haven’t been evicted once. I wish I drank less. But I’ve been strong, I’ve been working. I hang around with people older than me and they don’t necessarily have something of their own. They see me, and they’re like, ‘You’re ill. You’re getting up and going to work every day. You’re holding it down.’ But am I happy? I’ve experienced glimpses of happiness, but I’ve never been truly happy. I still battle a lot of things. The other day I woke up screaming, like fuck! But I’ve got to be here for something. I have a friend named Dre; he knows things about me, and he says: ‘For you to still be here— you’re here for a reason. You’ve got to see it through to the end— to find out what it all means.’ What I’d really love is to finally have some freedom one day. Not having to think about what I’m going to eat tomorrow, things like that. I feel like it’s coming at some point. And when it does, I’m going straight back to my aunt and uncle. No anger, nothing. Because I want them to be free too. They were also abused, mind you. They showed me the marks. My aunt also tried to commit suicide. They were never happy. They were never free. But they tried their hardest to survive. They still tried for me, I know that. And if I ever get some freedom, if I ever get some happiness, I want them to feel it too.”

caption: “I ran for City Council ten years ago in Eastern Queens, and a young man named Zohran Mamdani volunteered for my campaign. We were both part of a huge immigrant community of South Asian Muslims. Our community is such an important part of this city, but at the time we were not considered to be reliable voters. And that perception came with consequences. After 9/11 there were legal abuses against Muslims that would not have happened to any other community—because we lacked political power. Our campaign set out to transform the electorate. We tried to turn nonvoters into voters. Both of us were young: I was thirty-one, Zohran was twenty-three. And while most of our friends were out partying, we knocked on thousands of doors. But we learned that it’s the hardest sale in the world to make people care as much as you do. In the end I lost badly to a candidate endorsed by the Democratic political machine. The experience left me feeling jaded. There were times I wondered if the only way for a candidate to win was to work within a political machine. But here’s the problem with machines—they don’t have clear values. Our campaign had clear values: we wanted to bring power to people who didn’t have power. But the machine is already powerful, and it only cares about maintaining power. It’s not about new thinking. It’s not about change. If you become their candidate, you must give them loyalty regardless of their positions, and too many times those positions come from special interests. The whole process can make you cynical, which is why these last few months have been so emotional for me. This time around I was the one supporting Zohran, as campaign counsel. I’m filled with pride for what he’s achieved, using many of the lessons we learned ten years ago. I have no problem saying he’s a tremendously better candidate than I ever was. He speaks to people in ways I never could. But his success has given new meaning to all our hard work, so many years ago— knocking on doors, meeting with community elders. My campaign might not have been the swing of the axe that knocked down the tree— the first swing rarely is. But it turns out we were breaking ground for something bigger.”

caption: Eleven years ago I received a DM from some guy named Lin-Manuel Miranda. I’d never heard of him. He had about 30,000 Twitter followers at the time. He’d created a critically acclaimed show called ‘In The Heights,’ but I wasn’t fluent enough with Broadway for that to ring a bell. In his DM he told me to ‘holler’ at him if I ever came up to Washington Heights. A few weeks later, that’s exactly what I did. Why? Because I needed a Spanish interpreter, and I wanted to know if he’d consider accompanying me while I collected stories. Lin informed me that this would not be possible, because he’d just come home from the hospital with his newborn son. ‘Oh, really?’ I asked. And that’s how I randomly took the first portrait of the brand-new Miranda family. Lin mentioned at the time that he was working on ‘some play about Alexander Hamilton.’ Four months later Hamilton would have its off-Broadway premiere at the Public Theater. And well, the rest is history. I’ve always treasured this small intersection I had with Lin before the rocket ship took off. Not because I got to watch him change. But because I got to watch how little he changed. He’s remained the same good man I met that day: enamored with his newborn son, enamored with his wife, enamored with life. He’s gone on to compose music for so many celebrated films, modeling that zest for life to millions of children around the world— including my own. (I’m a Moana man myself, with all due respect to the Family Madrigal.) But what I’ve most admired about Lin is how much he supports other people. I’m not sure I’ve ever seen someone use their platform to so consistently highlight and uplift fellow artists. In that vein, he immediately agreed when I asked if he’d drop by Dear New York to play the Steinway Concert Grand. He spent days trying to lower my expectations. ‘I’m not a pianist,’ he said. ‘All I can do is noodle on the keys.’ And that’s exactly what he did this morning. He ‘noodled’ his way into the memories and lives of hundreds of very surprised people in Grand Central Station. Thank you @lin_manuel , for always reaching behind you to lift others up. And thank you for being such an important part of Dear New York.

caption: Dear New York might be the largest public art installation in decades. All of Grand Central Station has been transformed into a celebration of the diversity and humanity of New York City. As part of Dear New York, there is a Steinway Concert Grand Piano in the center of the main concourse. During the day the piano is played by some of the world’s most talented pianists, selected by @juilliardschool . But after 10 pm something magical happens. The piano is made available (through a submission process) to all sorts of New Yorkers. The only requirement: a fierce passion for playing piano. There were well over a thousand submissions and only a small amount could be selected. But among these are some beautiful, beautiful stories. Dear New York closes this Sunday. It has been such a magical run.

caption: I’d like to conclude with one final story that I think captures the spirit of Dear New York. During the final hour before Sunday’s closing ceremony there was no performer scheduled on the Steinway Concert Grand, so I loudly invited everyone in the crowd to take a turn. About six or seven random New Yorkers stepped forward, bravely volunteering for this once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to play the world’s finest piano for a huge crowd of people in Grand Central Station. It was such a joyous and communal experience. Each person played one song. Everyone was at-least-a-little nervous, but everyone nailed it under the brightest possible spotlight. Eventually one of the producers whispered that it was time to wrap up, but before I could tell everyone ‘Goodnight,’ I noticed the tiniest little hand being raised. It belonged to a six-year-old girl wearing a denim jacket, sparkly cowboy boots, and a small plastic princess crown. I knelt down and asked her name; she told me ‘Charlotte.’ I asked Charlotte if she wanted a chance to play, and she nodded with conviction. Her mother— half-proud, half-terrified—quickly told me that Charlotte had a keyboard at home, but had never played piano before. This small distinction did not bother Charlotte one bit. With the confidence of Liberace, she marched up to the Steinway, took a seat, and played piano for the very first time, in front of hundreds of people. I’m not sure anyone beyond the first row could hear it. But I am sure that everyone could feel it. Immediately following her performance, two hundred young singers from The Young People’s Chorus of New York City brought Dear New York to a close with an epic performance. (Video clip in carousel.) Thank you Charlotte, thank you @ypcofnyc, and thank you everyone, for being such an important part of Dear New York.

caption: I have a confession to make. I have not been 100 percent truthful. All week, in interviews and social media posts, I have been repeating the false claim that Dear New York has transformed ‘all of Grand Central’ into a piece of art celebrating the people and community of this city. I got a little caught up in the hype. This statement was not exactly true, and I apologize. I would now like to correct the record. Dear New York has entirely transformed the historic main concourse. It has transformed every level of the massive Grand Central subway system with an immersive installation designed by @trabuccocampos and his team at @pentagramdesign. It has transformed 150 digital screens, and all available signage into a celebration of the people of this city. It has filled the air with musical programming from @juilliardschool. It has transformed Grand Central’s stunning Vanderbilt Hall into a ‘crowd favorite’ exhibit  designed by @davidkorins which blends the work of 600 student artists with established artists, including the living legend @jamelshabazz. But here is where I got a little carried away. If you were one of the tens of thousands of people who became part of Dear New York yesterday, you might have noticed that the Vanderbilt Hall exhibit was closed. Alas, the truth cannot stay buried long: Dear New York was unable to secure 100 percent of Grand Central for the entirety of these two weeks. Exactly one thing was already on the calendar. Last night, Saturday October 11th, the first wedding Grand Central has seen in fifteen years took place in Vanderbilt Hall. But oh, what a beautiful inconvenience. Because how could you possibly celebrate the diversity and humanity of this city…. without a wedding. Congratulations to David and Meredith Garrett. Thank you for taking a small break from your big night, stepping out from behind the curtain, and becoming an important part of Dear New York.

caption: Last night someone asked me what part of Dear New York I’m proudest of; this was hard to answer. But I can tell you what’s filled my heart the most. Many in the press are calling it ‘The Children’s Exhibit,’ because Dear New York’s Vanderbilt Hall features the work of six hundred NYC student artists. Each student was asked to photograph and write about someone who has made a difference in their lives. Some of these artists are as young as four, and their photography might not be the most technically polished, but there is a striking intimacy that can only come from photographing someone you love. The written profiles which accompany the photographs are extremely touching, and collectively represent the millions of invisible, unsung heroes that form the bedrock of NYC’s community. It’s not the mayors and the movie stars that form the heart of this city. It’s the mothers, the fathers, the teachers, the social workers, and the millions of other people who show up every day in the lives of others. One reason the ‘Children’s Exhibit’ lands so deeply is that its amplified by a sister exhibition featuring eleven highly notable NYC photographers. Among them are living legends such as @jamelshabazz , a trailblazer in street portraiture. As well as Gugenheim Fellow @sarabennettbrooklyn , a former public defender who profiles formerly-incarcerated women. The two exhibits are blended seamlessly in an innovative, immersive design by @davidkorins . The most beautiful part of these blended exhibits is that all 611 artists— young and old, beginning and established— have been given the same museum-quality framing and presentation. The result is an egalitarian, non-hierarchical ode to the diversity, humanity, and community of this city.  The exhibit has been overflowing all week, from open to close, and I’m not sure I’ve ever seen an art installation elicit so much emotion. Dear New York closes on Sunday. For everyone who attends the final Sunday, you will be able to meet all eleven featured professional artists, who will be there to greet visitors between 2 pm and 5 pm.

caption: We’ve lost a legend. Stephanie ‘Tanqueray’ Johnson passed away last night after suffering a severe stroke. She will be most remembered for holding the world in thrall with her no-holds-barred storytelling about life as a burlesque dancer in the 1970’s. Stephanie was a complicated person. Her public persona was irresistibly charismatic. Yet behind the scenes I’ve rarely met somebody who had such difficulty with close relationships. She was internationally adored, yet intensely lonely. She was desirous of companionship, yet quick to cut people out of her life over the smallest slights. Stephanie told me endless stories about how badly her mother treated her as a child, yet remained capable of exhibiting that same behavior toward others. People are complicated. And the longer you live, the more you realize the most inexcusable behavior often stems from the saddest traumas. There was always a little girl inside of Stephanie who never had a chance to feel safe. A little girl who learned at a young age that the best way to keep from getting hurt was to throw the first punch. But this little girl also had such a love of life. And despite her X-rated stories, and her sharp edges, was capable of such innocence. Stephanie slept with a teddy bear until the day she died. She’d melt in the presence of animals and babies. And until the very end, she laughed like a little girl. In the final weeks of her life all the hard edges melted away. All the defense mechanisms, the learned responses. She reverted back to the little girl she’d been before she’d gotten hurt. And that is the Stephanie that is smiling down on us right now. In her own words: ‘When I get to heaven I hope God shows me a movie of my life. But just the funny parts. Not the in-between parts, cause then we’d both start crying. Underneath all the laughs and the gags, it was always about one thing: survival. Tanqueray was a lot of fun. But Tanqueray was Stephanie. And Stephanie was a teenage runaway from Albany: doing what she needed to do, and being who she needed to be, to get what she needed to get.” I love ya, Steph. Thanks for taking me, and all of us, on the greatest ride of our lives.

caption: “A few years back I did a whole art show where the pieces were made of leather. I stapled the shit out of them until they were puffy and weird, like muscles filled with blood. Then I covered them with jewels. Didn’t sell a lot of them. Most people thought ‘What the fuck are these?’ At the opening of the show I noticed two women talking quietly to each other: one of them was full-figured, the other one was old. So I decided to eavesdrop. And they must have gone to art school, because I heard the big one say: ‘Look at these, they’re so beautiful. But they do nothing.’ I never went to art school, so I thought ‘Oh shit, they found out how stupid I am.’ It made me feel so dumb. When I was a kid I had a big head, a football head. I had to wear a helmet. And this woman gave me that ‘football head feeling’ all over again. I wanted to slug her. I wanted to scream: ‘My art does nothing? What the fuck is it supposed to do, vacuum your house?’ But my mother taught me to never burn a bridge. So instead of blowing it out my mouth, I took a deep breath. I said to myself: ‘Just wait, wait a minute. Gestate with negative things, like a shaman. Like a little magic man.’ I said to myself: ‘Maybe they’re right. Wouldn’t it be great if my paintings could do something?’ A few weeks later I ended up finding an old man named Carl who has a hoard of crystals that he sells by the pound. All of Carl’s crystals have healing ‘goo goo’ in them, so I bought $5,000 worth. You see? By holding my tongue, I got something. Those women gave me a gift with their bitchery. Now my paintings can heal and dazzle you at the same time.”

caption: Dear New York closes in four short days. It has been an absolutely magical and historic two weeks. But it is not yet a finished work. Dear New York is an immersive art installation by people, for people, and about people. Everyone who visits Grand Central Station becomes part of it. With the crowds seeming to grow 20% each passing day, the work continues to grow more and more meaningful. Come join us this weekend as Dear New York reaches full bloom. When you arrive you will find a Grand Central completely cleared of advertising. If you come by subway, you’ll enter through an immersive installation covering all three levels of Grand Central subway station, designed by @trabuccocampos and his team at @pentagramdesign. You’ll then emerge into an iconic main concourse which has been completely transformed with light projections into a showcase of NYC’s humanity. For the first time in history, the main concourse has also been transformed by two weeks of musical programming performed by the celebrated students and alumni of @juilliardschool . After taking in a performance, be sure to swing by Vanderbilt Hall to experience the most-visited, most-talked-about art exhibit in town, designed by the legendary @davidkorins , and featuring the work of eleven highly notable NYC photographers alongside the work of 600 school-aged student artists—every participant given the same museum-quality printing and framing by @pictonewyork .  At 8 PM on Sunday night, there will be a short closing ceremony featuring a performance by a 200-strong chorus from @ypcofnyc. Afterwards Dear New York will go dark forever. It is incredibly tragic that it must die so soon. But also, that’s the reason it’s so alive.
